name: Motorbike
description: A two-wheeled motorcycle or motor-driven cycle designed for or capable of travel off developed roads, such as a trail, enduro or motocross bike; an electric dirt bike that doesn't meet federal motor vehicle safety standards is a motorbike, one of Idaho's off-highway vehicles.

restrictions.rule: Two wheels, designed for or capable of traveling off developed roadways and highways; no limit on motor power or speed
Titled, but not registered for highway use

Needs an IDPR OHV certificate of number, a $12 sticker valid January 1 through December 31, to ride on trails, open riding areas, OHV roads and highways; one used only on private land for farming or snow removal is exempt
The sticker goes on the right fork, or on the restricted vehicle plate when it has one; a nonresident needs a $12 nonresident OHV user certificate instead
Riding on city, county or highway district roads open to OHVs also takes a restricted vehicle license plate, a valid driver's license and liability insurance

With the plate it may use highways that aren't state or interstate highways, state highways posted 60 mph or less within a city or a mile of it, and state highways posted 65 mph or less outside cities for up to 5 miles to link OHV trails or reach fuel, food, lodging or repairs
Never on interstates or full access-controlled state highways unless the transportation board designates a section, and no faster than the posted limit or 45 mph, whichever is less, on any highway

On roads on state or federal land, a rider under 16 may ride without a license when supervised by a licensed adult 18 or older within 300 feet, and on national forest roads must also carry proof of an IDPR-approved OHV safety course
Riders and passengers under 18 must wear a DOT-approved helmet, except on private property
Becomes a motorcycle, with highway registration and plates, when its owner fits it to meet federal motor vehicle safety standards and self-certifies the conversion on ITD form 3018
